gloss: The room where food is stored, prepared, and cooked.
examples: We finally remodeled the *kitchen* last spring.
He was standing in the *kitchen* making coffee.
Most of the apartments in that building have tiny *kitchens*.

gloss: The appliance with burners on top that you cook on.
examples: There's a pot of chili on the *stove*.
Don't leave the *stove* on when you go out.
Our old *stove* only has three burners that work.
contrast: Americans say stove or range; British English says cooker.

gloss: The closed compartment you bake or roast food in.
examples: Preheat the *oven* to 375.
The bread's been in the *oven* for forty minutes.
Both *ovens* died the week before Thanksgiving.
contrast: Written with an o but said UH-vun, rhyming with the first part of 'lovin'.

gloss: The appliance that keeps food cold.
examples: Put the milk back in the *refrigerator*.
The new *refrigerator* barely fit through the door.
Restaurant *refrigerators* run all night long.
contrast: The short form fridge is spelled with a d that the full word doesn't have.

gloss: An informal word for a refrigerator.
examples: There's nothing in the *fridge* but ketchup.
Stick the leftovers in the *fridge*.
We keep a second *fridge* out in the garage.

gloss: The compartment or appliance that keeps food frozen.
examples: I've got a bag of peas in the *freezer*.
The *freezer* needs defrosting again.
Chest *freezers* hold a lot more than you'd think.

gloss: An oven that heats food quickly with microwave radiation.
examples: Heat it in the *microwave* for two minutes.
Don't put anything metal in the *microwave*.
The dorm kitchen has two *microwaves* and one sink.

gloss: A machine that washes dishes automatically.
examples: Can you load the *dishwasher* before you leave?
The *dishwasher* is making that noise again.
Older apartments here don't come with *dishwashers*.

gloss: An electric machine that purees or liquefies food.
examples: She threw everything in the *blender* and hit puree.
The *blender* is loud enough to wake the neighbors.
Good *blenders* aren't cheap.

gloss: A small appliance that browns slices of bread.
examples: The *toaster* burns everything on setting five.
He dropped a bagel in the *toaster* and forgot about it.
We got two *toasters* as wedding gifts.

gloss: An electric machine with beaters for mixing batter and dough.
examples: Beat the butter and sugar with a *mixer* for three minutes.
Her stand *mixer* takes up half the counter.
Hand *mixers* work fine for most recipes.

gloss: A metal frame over a fire or gas flame for cooking food outdoors.
examples: Dad's out back firing up the *grill*.
We cooked the whole dinner on the *grill*.
The apartment complex has two *grills* by the pool.
contrast: In American English a grill is the outdoor barbecue; the heating element inside a US oven is the broiler, which the British call a grill.

gloss: The part of an oven that cooks food with heat from directly above.
examples: Put it under the *broiler* for two minutes to brown the top.
On this stove the *broiler* is the drawer underneath.
Watch it closely — *broilers* burn things in seconds.
contrast: An American broiler is a British grill; an American grill is the outdoor kind.

gloss: One of the cooking rings or elements on top of a stove.
examples: Move the pan to the back *burner*.
One *burner* on this stove never lights.
Turn the *burner* down before it boils over.

gloss: The basin with a faucet where you wash dishes and hands.
examples: There's a stack of dishes in the *sink*.
Just rinse it off in the *sink*.
The kitchen has a double *sink*.

gloss: The fitting you turn to let water out of a pipe.
examples: The *faucet* drips all night.
Turn the *faucet* off all the way.
We replaced both bathroom *faucets* last month.
contrast: Americans say faucet; British English says tap.

gloss: A covered pot with a spout for boiling water.
examples: Put the *kettle* on.
The *kettle* whistles when the water's ready.
Electric *kettles* boil water faster than the stove does.

gloss: The flat working surface along a kitchen wall.
examples: Wipe down the *countertop* when you're done.
Granite *countertops* were the big selling point.
Don't leave raw chicken sitting on the *countertop*.

gloss: A cupboard with shelves and a door, usually mounted on a wall.
examples: The glasses are in the *cabinet* above the sink.
We painted the kitchen *cabinets* white.
He couldn't reach the top *cabinet* without a chair.
contrast: In ordinary speech it collapses to two syllables: KAB-nut.

gloss: A small room or closet where dry food is kept.
examples: There's a box of pasta in the *pantry*.
Our *pantry* is really just a closet with shelves.
Older houses around here have walk-in *pantries*.

gloss: A sliding box built into a piece of furniture.
examples: The forks are in the top *drawer*.
That *drawer* sticks every single time.
He went through all the kitchen *drawers* looking for a corkscrew.
contrast: One syllable in American speech — it sounds like 'draw' with an r, not DRAW-er.

gloss: A frame of bars used to hold or cool things.
examples: Move the oven *rack* up one position.
Let the cookies cool on a wire *rack*.
The dish *rack* by the sink is always full.

gloss: An insulated container that keeps food and drinks cold away from home.
examples: We packed sandwiches and a *cooler* full of ice.
Grab me a soda out of the *cooler*.
They hauled two *coolers* down to the beach.

gloss: A device that crushes coffee, pepper, or spices into small pieces.
examples: Grind the beans fresh in a burr *grinder*.
There's a pepper *grinder* on every table.
Cheap *grinders* heat the coffee up too much.

gloss: A device that counts down and signals when cooking time is up.
examples: Set a *timer* for twelve minutes.
The *timer* went off and nobody heard it.
I run two *timers* when I'm cooking three things at once.

gloss: An instrument for measuring how hot something is.
examples: Stick a *thermometer* into the thickest part of the breast.
An instant-read *thermometer* is the best twenty dollars you'll spend.
Candy *thermometers* clip onto the side of the pot.
contrast: The stress jumps to the second syllable: thur-MAH-muh-tur, not THUR-mo-meter.

gloss: A device for weighing ingredients.
examples: A kitchen *scale* makes baking much more accurate.
Put the bowl on the *scale* and hit tare.
Digital *scales* are cheap now.
contrast: One device is a scale, singular, even though Russian весы is plural.

gloss: A deep round container with a handle for cooking on a stove.
examples: Bring a big *pot* of water to a boil.
She stirred the *pot* every few minutes.
All my *pots* are stacked in the bottom cabinet.

gloss: A shallow metal container used for frying or baking.
examples: Heat a little oil in the *pan*.
Pour the batter into a greased *pan*.
Nonstick *pans* don't last forever.

gloss: A heavy frying pan with sloping sides.
examples: Brown the onions in a cast-iron *skillet*.
He fried the eggs in the same *skillet*.
Those old *skillets* only get better with age.

gloss: A small deep pan with a single long handle.
examples: Melt the butter in a small *saucepan*.
The rice is in the *saucepan* on the back burner.
I only own two *saucepans*.

gloss: A deep bowl-shaped pan used for quick, high-heat cooking.
examples: Get the *wok* screaming hot before the vegetables go in.
A carbon steel *wok* costs about thirty bucks.
Most home stoves aren't hot enough for real *wok* cooking.

gloss: A dish of food baked slowly in a deep covered container.
examples: She brought a green bean *casserole* to the potluck.
Bake the *casserole* uncovered for the last ten minutes.
People kept dropping off *casseroles* all week.

gloss: A removable cover for a pot, pan, or container.
examples: Put the *lid* on and let it steam for five minutes.
The *lid* doesn't fit this pot.
Half our containers are missing *lids*.

gloss: A flat piece of metal, wood, or plastic used to carry or hold food.
examples: She carried the drinks out on a *tray*.
Line the *tray* with parchment first.
The ice *trays* are in the freezer door.

gloss: A bowl full of holes used for draining water off food.
examples: Drain the pasta in a *colander*.
Rinse the beans in a *colander* under cold water.
We own two *colanders* and I can never find either one.

gloss: A mesh device that separates solids from a liquid.
examples: Pour the stock through a fine-mesh *strainer*.
Use a *strainer* so the seeds don't get in.
Small *strainers* work better for loose tea.

gloss: A fine mesh screen for sifting dry ingredients or straining liquids.
examples: Push the sauce through a *sieve* to make it smooth.
Sift the flour through a *sieve* first.
The finest *sieves* clog almost immediately.
contrast: Rhymes with 'give' — SIV. The -ie- is not said 'ee'.

gloss: A metal tool with sharp holes for shredding food.
examples: Shred the cheese on the coarse side of the *grater*.
A box *grater* is easier to clean than it looks.
Both *graters* went through the dishwasher.
contrast: Sounds exactly like 'greater'.

gloss: A hand tool that strips the skin off vegetables and fruit.
examples: Peel the carrots with a vegetable *peeler*.
A sharp *peeler* saves a lot of time.
Y-shaped *peelers* are the ones most cooks prefer.

gloss: A loop-shaped wire tool for beating eggs or cream.
examples: Beat the eggs with a *whisk*.
Use a *whisk*, not a fork, or you'll get lumps.
Balloon *whisks* are the ones for whipping cream.

gloss: A flat tool for flipping food or scraping a bowl.
examples: Flip the pancakes with a *spatula*.
Scrape the bowl down with a rubber *spatula*.
I keep three *spatulas* in the crock by the stove.

gloss: A deep long-handled spoon for serving soup.
examples: Serve the soup with a *ladle*.
He filled each bowl with two *ladles* of chili.
The *ladle* is hanging on the hook by the stove.

gloss: A utensil with a shallow bowl on a handle, used for eating and stirring.
examples: Stir it with a wooden *spoon*.
I need a clean *spoon*.
All the *spoons* are dirty.

gloss: A utensil with prongs for picking up food.
examples: Test the potatoes with a *fork*.
He set a knife and *fork* at every place.
The *forks* go on the left.

gloss: A small spoon, or the amount of an ingredient it holds.
examples: Add a *teaspoon* of vanilla.
That's about two *teaspoons* of salt.
Level the *teaspoon* off with the back of a knife.

gloss: A large spoon, or the amount of an ingredient it holds.
examples: Melt two *tablespoons* of butter.
A *tablespoon* is three teaspoons.
Measure the oil with a real *tablespoon*, not a soup spoon.

gloss: A tool with a spiral point for pulling corks out of bottles.
examples: Does anybody have a *corkscrew*?
We opened it with a cheap *corkscrew* from the drawer.
Waiter's *corkscrews* are the easiest kind to use.

gloss: A cylinder used to flatten dough.
examples: Roll the dough out with a *rolling pin*.
Her *rolling pin* was her grandmother's.
Marble *rolling pins* stay cold, which helps with pastry.

gloss: A long pin that holds pieces of food together for grilling.
examples: Thread the shrimp onto a *skewer*.
Soak wooden *skewers* first so they don't burn.
He pulled the meat off the *skewer* with his fork.

gloss: A hollow container that gives food its shape as it sets.
examples: Pour the jelly into a *mold* and chill it overnight.
She turned the cake out of a bundt *mold*.
Silicone *molds* make it easy to get chocolate out.
contrast: American spelling is mold; British English writes mould.

gloss: A flat board you chop food on.
examples: Chop the onion on a *cutting board*, not on the counter.
Use a separate *cutting board* for raw meat.
Wooden *cutting boards* need oil once in a while.
contrast: Americans say cutting board; British English says chopping board.

gloss: A padded glove for handling hot pans.
examples: Grab an oven *mitt* before you touch that.
The *mitt* has a hole burned through the thumb.
Both *mitts* are in the drawer by the stove.

gloss: A garment tied over your clothes to keep them clean while cooking.
examples: He tied on an *apron* before he started.
There's flour all over your *apron*.
The restaurant hands out clean *aprons* every shift.

gloss: A soft absorbent block used for washing dishes and wiping surfaces.
examples: Wipe the counter with a damp *sponge*.
That *sponge* smells — just throw it out.
I buy *sponges* in packs of six.
contrast: Written -onge but said SPUNJ, rhyming with 'plunge'.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A soap-like cleaner used for washing dishes or clothes.
examples: Add a squirt of dish *detergent* to the water.
We're completely out of *detergent*.
The store-brand *detergents* work just as well.

gloss: Thin sheet metal used to wrap or cover food.
examples: Cover the pan with *foil* and bake it another hour.
Wrap the potatoes in *foil* before they go on the grill.
We're out of *foil* — use parchment instead.
contrast: Uncountable: a sheet of foil, never 'a foil' or 'foils' in the kitchen sense.

gloss: Heat-resistant paper used to line baking pans.
examples: Line the sheet pan with *parchment*.
The cookies won't stick if you use *parchment*.
One roll of *parchment* lasts me a year.

gloss: A small container with holes in the top for sprinkling salt or pepper.
examples: Pass me the salt *shaker*.
The pepper *shaker* is clogged again.
Every table in the diner had matching *shakers*.

gloss: A tall container with a handle and a spout for pouring drinks.
examples: She poured the lemonade out of a glass *pitcher*.
There's a *pitcher* of iced tea in the fridge.
They brought out two *pitchers* of water.
contrast: Americans say pitcher; British English says jug.

gloss: A large cup with a handle, used for hot drinks.
examples: He drank his coffee out of a chipped *mug*.
Pour it into a *mug* and microwave it.
All the *mugs* are in the dishwasher.

gloss: The small shallow plate that a cup sits on.
examples: The cup came with a matching *saucer*.
She set her spoon down on the *saucer*.
The *saucers* are stacked behind the cups.

gloss: A large flat plate for serving food to several people.
examples: Arrange the cheese on a wooden *platter*.
He carried the turkey out on a big *platter*.
They sent over two *platters* of sandwiches.

gloss: A container you serve food in, or a particular prepared food.
examples: Somebody has to do the *dishes*.
Rice is the main *dish* at almost every meal there.
Bake it in an oven-safe *dish*.

gloss: A piece of cloth or paper used at the table to wipe your hands and mouth.
examples: Grab a *napkin* — you've got sauce on your chin.
She folded a cloth *napkin* at each place.
The *napkins* are in the top drawer.

gloss: A cloth spread over a table before a meal.
examples: Spread a *tablecloth* over the picnic table.
Somebody spilled wine on the *tablecloth*.
They save the good *tablecloths* for holidays.

gloss: The knives, forks, and spoons used at a meal.
examples: Set out the *silverware* while I finish the salad.
There's *silverware* in the drawer by the sink.
He ran out of clean *silverware* halfway through the party.
contrast: Uncountable — never 'a silverware' or 'silverwares'. British English says cutlery.

gloss: Pots and pans considered together.
examples: They registered for a whole set of *cookware*.
Cast iron is the cheapest good *cookware* you can buy.
Most nonstick *cookware* can't go in the dishwasher.
contrast: Uncountable, like equipment: a piece of cookware, never 'cookwares'.

gloss: A tool used in preparing or eating food.
examples: Use a wooden *utensil* so you don't scratch the pan.
The drawer is jammed with *utensils* nobody ever uses.
Bring your own *utensils* to the picnic.
contrast: Stress is on the second syllable: yoo-TEN-sul.

gloss: A machine designed for a household job such as cooking or washing.
examples: The kitchen comes with all new *appliances*.
That *appliance* draws a lot of power.
They deliver large *appliances* on Tuesdays.

gloss: A pair of thin sticks used for eating in much of East Asia.
examples: He still can't eat with *chopsticks*.
They gave us plastic forks instead of *chopsticks*.
A pair of *chopsticks* came with every order.
contrast: Normally plural, since you use two: a pair of chopsticks.

gloss: A thin tube you drink through.
examples: Can I get a *straw* with that?
She stirred her iced coffee with the *straw*.
The place switched to paper *straws* last year.

gloss: A tiny piece that breaks off bread or a cookie.
examples: There's a *crumb* on your lip.
He brushed the *crumbs* off the counter.
The bottom of the toaster is full of *crumbs*.
contrast: The b is silent: KRUM.

gloss: The activity of preparing food, or a particular style of it.
examples: He does most of the *cooking* at home.
Italian *cooking* uses far fewer ingredients than people think.
*Cooking* for eight people takes some planning.

gloss: The activity of cooking bread, cakes, and pastry in an oven.
examples: She got into *baking* during the pandemic.
*Baking* is more exact than cooking — you can't just eyeball it.
He's much better at *baking* than at anything on the stove.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: An outdoor meal cooked over fire, or the smoked meat itself.
examples: They're having a *barbecue* Saturday afternoon.
We drove two hours for that *barbecue*.
Summer around here is nothing but *barbecues* and baseball.
contrast: The event is countable (two barbecues); the food is uncountable (some barbecue). Also spelled barbeque or BBQ.

gloss: A large piece of meat cooked in an oven.
examples: She put a *roast* in the oven before church.
The *roast* came out dry.
Pot *roasts* are cheap and hard to ruin.

gloss: Meat and vegetables cooked slowly in liquid.
examples: There's beef *stew* in the slow cooker.
A *stew* always tastes better the next day.
Winter is for soups and *stews*.
contrast: Americans say STOO; the British say STYOO.

ru: кипение (в оборотах bring to a boil)
gloss: The state of a liquid bubbling at its highest temperature.
examples: Bring the water to a *boil* before you add the pasta.
The soup came to a *boil* faster than I expected.
Turn it down as soon as you get a rolling *boil*.

ru: слабое кипение, томление на медленном огне
gloss: Gentle cooking in liquid just below boiling.
examples: Reduce the heat and hold it at a *simmer*.
Bring the sauce to a *simmer*, then cover it.
A slow *simmer* pulls a lot more flavor out of the bones.

gloss: A set of instructions for making a particular dish.
examples: Do you have the *recipe* for that cake?
The *recipe* calls for buttermilk.
She writes all her *recipes* on index cards.
contrast: Three syllables, REH-suh-pee — the final -e is pronounced.

gloss: One of the foods that go into a dish.
examples: Read the *ingredients* on the label.
The only *ingredient* I'm missing is cilantro.
Good bread has four *ingredients*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Salt, pepper, or other flavorings added to food.
examples: Taste it and adjust the *seasoning*.
The chicken needs more *seasoning*.
He keeps his *seasonings* in a drawer, not on a rack.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A strongly flavored substance from a plant, used in cooking.
examples: Add the *spices* and let them toast for a minute.
Cinnamon is the only *spice* in it.
There's not enough *spice* in this.

gloss: A leafy plant such as basil or parsley used to flavor food.
examples: Fresh *herbs* make a huge difference.
Which *herb* goes in pesto?
She grows *herbs* on the windowsill.
contrast: In American English the h is silent: URB. The British say HURB.

gloss: Ground grain used for baking.
examples: Add the *flour* a cup at a time.
There's *flour* all over the counter.
We're out of *flour* again.
contrast: Sounds exactly like 'flower'.

gloss: A thick mixture of flour and liquid, kneaded before baking.
examples: Let the *dough* rise for an hour.
The *dough* is too sticky — add a little more flour.
She rolled the *dough* out thin.
contrast: The -ough is just OH and the gh is silent: DOH.

gloss: A thin pourable mixture of flour, egg, and liquid.
examples: Pour the *batter* into the pan.
Don't overmix the *batter* or the muffins get tough.
Pancake *batter* should be a little lumpy.

gloss: A living fungus used to make bread rise.
examples: The recipe calls for a packet of *yeast*.
Check that the *yeast* is still active.
Bread made without *yeast* comes out flat.
contrast: Uncountable in English, though Russian дрожжи is plural: some yeast, not 'yeasts'.

gloss: A thin savory liquid made by simmering meat or vegetables.
examples: Simmer the vegetables in chicken *broth*.
Add a little more *broth* if it gets too thick.
The store-bought *broths* are all too salty.

gloss: A thick liquid served with or on food.
examples: The pasta needs more *sauce*.
He makes a killer barbecue *sauce*.
They served it with three different *sauces*.

gloss: A sauce made from the juices that come out of cooking meat.
examples: Pour the *gravy* over the mashed potatoes.
She makes *gravy* from the pan drippings.
There isn't enough *gravy* for everybody.

gloss: A sauce of oil and vinegar or cream poured over salad.
examples: What kind of *dressing* do you want on your salad?
Toss the greens with the *dressing* right before you serve it.
The house *dressings* are all made from scratch.

gloss: A seasoned liquid that food soaks in before cooking.
examples: Let the chicken sit in the *marinade* overnight.
The *marinade* is just soy sauce, garlic, and ginger.
Acidic *marinades* will start to cook the fish.
contrast: The noun is marinade (MEH-ruh-nayd); the verb is marinate (MEH-ruh-nayt).

gloss: A shiny coating brushed or poured over food.
examples: Brush a honey *glaze* over the ham.
The donuts have a thin sugar *glaze*.
Sweet *glazes* burn if the oven's too hot.

gloss: A small decorative addition placed on a finished dish.
examples: The parsley is just a *garnish*.
He added a lemon twist as a *garnish*.
Skip the *garnishes* if you're in a hurry.
contrast: False friend: an English garnish is a decoration on the plate, not a Russian «гарнир», which is a side dish.

gloss: The hard outer layer of bread, or the pastry shell of a pie.
examples: The *crust* came out too pale.
She buys the *crust* instead of making it.
He cuts the *crusts* off his kid's sandwiches.

gloss: The food put inside a pie, sandwich, or pastry.
examples: The *filling* is mostly apples and cinnamon.
Let the *filling* cool before you put the top crust on.
They make three different *fillings*.

gloss: Food put on top of another food for flavor.
examples: What *toppings* do you want on the pizza?
The crumb *topping* is the best part.
Extra *toppings* are a dollar each.

gloss: Food remaining after a meal that gets eaten later.
examples: We ate *leftovers* three nights in a row.
Take some *leftovers* home with you.
There weren't any *leftovers* — they cleaned it out.
contrast: Almost always plural: leftovers, not 'a leftover'.

gloss: The amount of food served to one person.
examples: The *portions* at that place are huge.
Cut the dough into eight equal *portions*.
A single *portion* is about a cup.

gloss: One standard helping of food, as counted in a recipe.
examples: This recipe makes four *servings*.
One *serving* is around 300 calories.
He went back for a second *serving*.

gloss: An occasion of eating, such as breakfast or dinner.
examples: Breakfast is my favorite *meal*.
We eat three *meals* a day.
That was the best *meal* I've had all year.

gloss: One part of a meal served separately from the others.
examples: The main *course* was salmon.
Dinner was five *courses* and took three hours.
We skipped the dessert *course*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like 'coarse', which means rough.

gloss: A small dish eaten before the main course.
examples: We ordered a couple of *appetizers* to share.
The shrimp *appetizer* is worth it.
He filled up on *appetizers* before the entrée even came.
contrast: Americans say appetizer; the British say starter.

gloss: The sweet course served at the end of a meal.
examples: What's for *dessert*?
She skipped *dessert* and just had coffee.
They have four *desserts* on the menu.
contrast: Two s's, stress on the second syllable: dih-ZURT. One s and first-syllable stress gives desert (DEZ-urt), the dry place.

gloss: A meal where dishes are laid out and guests serve themselves.
examples: The hotel does a breakfast *buffet* until ten.
We hit the *buffet* twice.
Chinese *buffets* were everywhere in that town.
contrast: The t is silent and the stress is on the second syllable: buh-FAY.

gloss: A style of cooking associated with a country or region.
examples: He's obsessed with Thai *cuisine*.
The restaurant serves modern American *cuisine*.
French *cuisine* isn't all heavy sauces.
contrast: Said kwih-ZEEN: the c is a k sound and the s sounds like z.

ru: вкус, привкус; сорт (мороженого и т. п.)
countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: How something tastes, or one variety of a food sold in several tastes.
examples: This sauce has no *flavor* at all.
They had twelve *flavors* of ice cream.
Roasting brings out the *flavor* of the vegetables.
contrast: American spelling is flavor; British English writes flavour.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The sensation food produces in your mouth, or a small sample of it.
examples: It has a slightly bitter *taste*.
A bad cold ruins your sense of *taste*.
Give me a *taste* before you add more salt.

gloss: A pleasant smell, especially of food or drink.
examples: The *aroma* of garlic filled the whole apartment.
Coffee has a stronger *aroma* than it does taste.
The *aromas* coming out of that kitchen were unbelievable.

gloss: The way food feels in the mouth.
examples: The bread has a nice chewy *texture*.
Overcooking ruins the *texture* of shrimp.
The two sauces have completely different *textures*.

gloss: How hot or cold something is, measured in degrees.
examples: Bring the butter to room *temperature* first.
Check the internal *temperature* with a thermometer.
Ovens hold *temperatures* differently, so watch the food, not the clock.
contrast: Normally three syllables in speech: TEM-pruh-chur.

gloss: The level of warmth used to cook something.
examples: Cook it over medium *heat*.
Turn the *heat* down before it scorches.
Cast iron holds *heat* better than aluminum.

gloss: The hot vapor that rises from boiling water.
examples: Lift the lid away from you so the *steam* doesn't burn you.
The rice finishes cooking in its own *steam*.
There was so much *steam* the windows fogged up.

gloss: An amount of food made or baked at one time.
examples: The first *batch* of cookies burned.
She makes a big *batch* of soup on Sundays.
We froze two *batches* of sauce.

gloss: Ingredients that have been combined together.
examples: Stir the *mixture* until it's smooth.
Pour the *mixture* over the crust.
Both *mixtures* need to chill for an hour.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The outer skin of a fruit or vegetable.
examples: Grate a little orange *peel* into the batter.
He slipped on a banana *peel*.
